opening.spoken: This record covers the claimed solution of Erdős problem #306: what has been claimed, what it rests on, and what would have to be checked by whom.

short_version.spoken: Erdős and Graham asked whether every positive rational with squarefree denominator is a sum of distinct unit fractions whose denominators are products of two distinct primes. In September 2026 Shisheng Li listed a claimed full proof with an arXiv paper and a Lean development, building on a June 2026 Lean development by Yuren Tang that proved the result conditional on two stated axioms. A third-party formalisation of the problem statement exists, so part of the semantic check can be done by machine. On 2026-11-14 Nervous Machine built the Lean development at its pinned commit on an independent machine, with the standard axioms only, and showed by machine that it proves the third-party statement word for word. Nobody independent has read that statement against the problem as posed, or the paper.

what_happened.spoken: The claim was pinned from the public record. Nervous Machine then wrote down five checks and their predicted outcomes, fetched the Lean development at the pinned commit inside a virtual machine, built it, scanned it, printed the main theorem's axioms with its own file, and closed the third party's statement of the problem with the claimant's theorem. All five held. What remains is human: does the formal statement say what Erdős and Graham asked, and does the paper's argument hold as written. A reading guide now lays the formal statement beside the problem as posed, definition by definition, so the human read takes under an hour.

the claimant's own README reports that the Lean development follows the paper lemma by lemma and that the formalisation replaced the paper's cited Ramanujan inequality with a proved bound; a reader of the paper should start there

cycles.spoken: Shisheng Li posted an arXiv paper showing that every natural number is a sum of distinct semiprime unit fractions, a partial result toward the problem. Terence Tao's Erdős-problems AI wiki listed a candidate full solution with Lean by Yuren Tang, marked unverified; Tang's Lean development is deposited on Zenodo and is conditional on two stated axioms. Shisheng Li posted an arXiv paper claiming an elementary full proof. Shisheng Li published the Lean development on GitHub and listed the proof claim on the problem page, reporting no sorry, standard axioms only, and a proof of the third-party formal statement. The problem page lists one proof claim, not marked accepted by the site; the repository has no licence file.

cycles.spoken: Nervous Machine fetched Shisheng Li's Lean development for problem 306 at the pinned commit, inside a virtual machine, and built it with the toolchain and Mathlib version it pins. The build finished in under a minute with no errors, and our own axiom print shows the main theorem resting on the three standard axioms only. We then copied the problem's statement from Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository, word for word, into our own file and closed it with the claimant's theorem in one step. So the machine part of the semantic question is settled: the claimant proved exactly the third party's statement. Whether that statement is the problem Erdős and Graham posed is still a question for a mathematician.

preregistered.question: Can the open semantic gap (EG2) be made cheaper for a human reviewer: the problem as posed, the third-party formal statement, every definition behind it, a plain rendering, and the points to confirm?
preregistered.rule: Statements quoted verbatim from the pinned files with file and line; renderings marked as the agent's; every discrepancy recorded whether harmless or not; worked examples checked by Lean, not asserted; standing unchanged by construction.
predictions: P1: the formal statement renders to the page's sentence with no constant or quantifier mismatch
P2: at least one boundary convention needs a sentence (k = 0, division by zero, Squarefree 1); none changes the meaning

cycles.spoken: Nervous Machine wrote the reading guide for the one question on this record that a machine cannot settle: whether the formal statement of problem 306 says what Erdős and Graham asked. The guide quotes the problem page and the third-party formal statement word for word, traces every symbol in it to its definition in Mathlib or Lean's core with file and line, gives a plain reading of each piece, and has Lean itself check eight small examples, such as which small numbers count as a product of two distinct primes. Seven conventions are written down, including one where Lean's index numerals wrap for the empty case; none changes the meaning in the agent's reading. The readings are the system's, not a mathematician's, so nothing changed standing. A number theorist can now sign or refuse four lines in under an hour.

background.spoken: Take any positive rational a/b whose denominator b is squarefree. Can a/b always be written as a sum of distinct unit fractions 1/n, each n the product of two distinct primes? The case of three distinct primes with b = 1 was settled by Butler, Erdős and Graham in 2015; many explicit decompositions of 1 are known.

background.spoken: The claim is a full solution: every a/b with b squarefree is a finite sum of distinct 1/(pq) with p and q distinct primes. After reducing to small targets it uses one complete bipartite graph between a set of small primes and a tuned set of larger primes, counts subgraphs with the right reciprocal sum modulo one by a finite Fourier sum, and needs only Chebyshev-type bounds on primes. The author reports a Lean formalisation with no sorry and standard axioms only, which also proves the third-party formal-conjectures statement, and notes that version 1 of the arXiv paper still says the formalisation assumed Ramanujan's inequality while the repository now proves the needed bound. The author describes the argument as using Yuren Tang's circle-method framework with a different construction. Tang's own Lean development, deposited on Zenodo, gave a proof conditional on two Rosser–Schoenfeld-type axioms; the Erdős wiki listed it as a candidate full solution with Lean on June 19, 2026.
